lessons.title: extends, super & constructor chaining
lessons.summary: Subclasses, implicit super() and constructor order.

blocks.text: `extends` makes a class a **subclass**. It inherits the parent's fields and methods and can add its own.

items: A class extends exactly **one** class. Without `extends`, it extends `java.lang.Object`.
Inherited: `public` and `protected` members, plus package-private ones when in the same package.
Not inherited: `private` members and constructors.
A `final` class can't be extended (`String` is final).

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python allows `class Dog(Animal, Pet)`. A Java class has exactly one parent class. Extra types come from interfaces (lesson 9).

steps.prompt: Make Cat a subclass of Animal.
steps.explanation: Classes use `extends` for a parent class. `implements` is for interfaces, and Python's `class Cat(Animal)` / C#'s `:` don't exist in Java.

blocks.text: Constructors are **not** inherited. Every constructor begins by calling another constructor: `this(...)` in the same class or `super(...)` in the parent. If you write neither, the compiler inserts `super();`.

blocks.caption: The parent part is always built first.

blocks.title: Read it like a stack
blocks.text: The calls go **up** to `Object` first. The constructor bodies then finish from the top of the hierarchy **down**.

Add static and instance initializers and the full order is: each class's `static` init runs **once**, parent first, the first time the class is used. Then, for **every** `new`: parent instance fields and blocks, parent constructor body, child instance fields and blocks, child constructor body.

blocks.caption: Static parts print once; the instance parts repeat for each new.

verify.value:
Bs Ds Bi Bc Di Dc
Bi Bc Di Dc

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `new Q()` runs `Q()`, which calls `this(5)`. `Q(int)` calls `super(5)`, so `P(int)` runs, which calls `this()`. `P()` prints **1** first. Then each body finishes in reverse call order: P(int) prints 2, Q(int) prints 4, Q() prints 3.

steps.title: When the parent has no no-arg constructor

blocks.text: Once a class declares **any** constructor, the compiler no longer generates the default no-arg one. A subclass that relies on the implicit `super()` then fails to compile.
`Car` has no constructor, so it gets a default one: `Car() { super(); }`. But `Vehicle()` doesn't exist. Fix it by calling the constructor that does exist:

blocks.title: No constructor written is still a call
blocks.text: An empty subclass still calls `super()` through its default constructor. Check the parent: does it have a no-arg constructor?

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Both `Leaf(int)` and `Top(int)` get an implicit `super()`. For Leaf that's `Mid()`, which exists. For Top that's `Base()`, which doesn't: Base only has `Base(int)`. The parameter `n` of Top's constructor is not passed up automatically.

items: `super(...)` or `this(...)` must be the **first statement** in the constructor.
A constructor contains one of them, never both.
Arguments to `super(...)` can't use the object's own instance fields or instance methods (static ones are fine).
`super.method()` calls the parent's version of a method. It can appear anywhere in an instance method.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Newer Java versions are relaxing the "must be first" rule. The 1Z0-830 exam is **Java 21**: `super(...)` and `this(...)` must come first.

blocks.title: Constants are already there
blocks.text: A `final` field initialized with a **constant expression** (a literal, or `"a" + 1`) is a compile-time constant, and the compiler inlines its value. So an overridden method called from the parent constructor sees `5` or `"hi"`, not `0` or `null`. A `final` field set by a method call is an ordinary field and still holds its default at that point.

steps.prompt: Given `class Base { Base(String s) { } }`, which two constructors compile in `class Sub extends Base`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Base has only `Base(String)`, so every Sub constructor must call `super(someString)` as its first statement. `Sub() { }` gets an implicit `super()`, which doesn't exist; same for an explicit `super()`. A statement before `super(...)` is illegal in Java 21.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: The object is a Circle, so `s.name()` runs Circle's version. Inside it, `super.name()` explicitly calls Shape's version, which returns "shape". There is no recursion: `super.` skips the override.

steps.prompt: Order the lines to make a Dog constructor that compiles.
steps.explanation: `super(n)` must be the first statement, so it comes before the print. Animal only has `Animal(String)`, so an argument-less `super()` would not compile.

steps.prompt: A constructor may call `this(...)` on its first line and `super(...)` on its second line.
steps.explanation: Both must be the first statement, so a constructor can have at most one of them. A `this(...)` call delegates to another constructor, which will call `super(...)` itself.

lessons.title: Overriding rules
lessons.summary: Signature, access, return type, exceptions, hiding.

blocks.text: A subclass **overrides** an instance method by declaring one with the same name and parameter types. Which version runs is decided by the **object**, not the variable type.

rows: Exactly the same (otherwise it's an overload)
Same or a subtype (covariant). Primitives must match exactly
Same or wider: private < package < protected < public
None, the same, or narrower. Never new or broader

blocks.title: Use @Override
blocks.text: `@Override` makes the compiler check that the method really overrides something. A typo like `tostring()` then fails to compile instead of silently adding a new method.

blocks.title: Beyond the core objectives: other annotations
blocks.text: `@Deprecated(since = "9", forRemoval = true)` only makes callers get a compiler **warning**; the code still compiles and runs. `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` silences warnings. `@FunctionalInterface` demands exactly one abstract method, and defaults and statics are still allowed. `@SafeVarargs` is legal only on constructors and on `static`, `final` or `private` varargs methods.

items: `protected` → `public`: wider access.
`Object` → `String`: covariant return.
`IOException` → `FileNotFoundException`: narrower checked exception.

blocks.title: Think "a caller of the parent"
blocks.text: Code written against `Reader` must keep working with a `TextReader`. So the override may promise **more** (wider access, more specific return) but never throw **more**.

steps.prompt: Which two methods compile when placed in class B? Choose two.
options: protected Number get() throws Exception { return 2; }
public Number get() throws FileNotFoundException { return 2; }
steps.explanation: Option A widens access and returns a subtype of Number (no exception is fine). Option E widens access and throws a narrower checked exception. Package access is weaker than protected; `Object` is not a subtype of `Number`; `Exception` is broader than `IOException`; and `long` is a primitive, not a Number.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: `move()` is public in Animal. Overriding it with package access makes it **less** visible, which is illegal. Lines 7 and 8 widen access (package → protected, protected → public), which is allowed.

blocks.text: A static method with the same signature in a subclass **hides** the parent's. No dynamic dispatch: the **reference type** decides which one is called.

items: instance overrides instance: dynamic dispatch on the object.
static hides static: chosen by the reference type at compile time.
Mixing (static in one, instance in the other) is a compile error.
Fields are never overridden. A same-named field **hides** the parent's and is also chosen by the reference type.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: The reference type is Parent. Fields (`p.name`) and static methods (`p.kind()`) are hidden, not overridden, so Parent's versions are used. `who()` is an instance method, so the Child override runs, and inside Child `name` means Child's field.

items: `private` methods aren't inherited. A same-signature method in the subclass is a new, unrelated method, and `@Override` on it fails.
`final` methods can't be overridden (or hidden).
Constructors aren't inherited, so they're never overridden.

blocks.title: Private + polymorphism
blocks.text: When a parent method calls its own **private** method, the parent's version always runs, no matter what the subclass declares.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `id()` in Base is private, so Derived's `id()` doesn't override it. Inside `show()` the call `id()` is bound to Base's private method. If Base's `id()` were package-private, the output would be "derived".

steps.prompt: A subclass method with the same signature as a `private` parent method compiles when it is marked `@Override`.
steps.explanation: Private methods are not inherited, so there is nothing to override. `@Override` makes the compiler check that, and it reports an error. Without the annotation the method compiles as a brand new method.

steps.prompt: Which statement is true?
options: Compilation fails because `int` is not the same return type as `long`.
steps.explanation: Covariant returns only apply to reference types. For primitives the override must return exactly the same type, so `int power()` can't override `long power()`. `start()` is final, but Turbo doesn't try to override it, so that's fine.

steps.prompt: Complete the override so it is checked by the compiler and widens access.
steps.explanation: The annotation is `@Override` (no s). `public` is wider than Doc's package access. `private` would be weaker, and `static` can't hide an instance method. Returning `Pdf` instead of `Object` is a legal covariant return.

lessons.title: Abstract classes
lessons.summary: Partial classes, abstract methods and illegal combinations.

blocks.text: An `abstract` class is a partial design. You can't create it with `new`, and it can declare `abstract` methods: methods with no body that subclasses must implement.

items: An abstract class can have constructors, fields, concrete methods, and even **zero** abstract methods.
A class with any abstract method must itself be `abstract`.
The first **concrete** subclass must implement every inherited abstract method. An abstract subclass may leave them.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: With Python's `ABC` and `@abstractmethod`, instantiating fails at **runtime** with a TypeError. Java rejects `new Shape(...)` at **compile** time.

steps.prompt: Complete the declarations.
steps.explanation: A method without a body must be `abstract`, and a class with an abstract method must be `abstract` too. `final` would forbid the subclass, `default` is for interface methods, and a `static` method can't be implemented by a subclass.

rows: final forbids subclasses; abstract needs them
a final method can never be implemented
private isn't inherited, so no one can implement it

blocks.title: An empty body is a body
blocks.text: `abstract void m() { }` fails because `{ }` is a body. The correct form ends with a semicolon: `abstract void m();`.

steps.prompt: Which two declarations compile? Choose two.
options: abstract class A { abstract void m(); }
abstract class A { abstract void m() { } }
abstract class A { private abstract void m(); }
steps.explanation: An abstract class may have abstract methods, or none at all. An abstract method can't have a body, can't live in a non-abstract class, and can't be private. `abstract final` contradicts itself.

blocks.text: A concrete method in the abstract class can call an abstract one. At runtime the subclass's implementation runs. This is the **template method** pattern.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Creating a Sales runs Report's constructor first (an abstract class still has one), printing R, then Sales's prints S. `print()` calls the abstract `body()`, which dispatches to Sales.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Hammer is abstract, so `new Hammer()` is illegal even though it has no abstract methods of its own. Hammer may skip `use()` because it's abstract; Mallet is the first concrete class and implements it. Line 10 is fine: an abstract type works as a reference type.

steps.prompt: An abstract class can declare a constructor.
steps.explanation: You can't call `new` on an abstract class, but its constructor still runs whenever a subclass is created, via `super(...)`. It typically initializes the shared fields.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Fish is concrete but implements only `name()`. It inherits the abstract `age()` without implementing it, so `class Fish` fails to compile. Either implement `age()` or declare Fish `abstract`.

lessons.title: Polymorphism & casting
lessons.summary: Reference type vs object type, casts and ClassCastException.

blocks.text: In `Animal a = new Dog();` the **reference type** is `Animal` (what the compiler sees) and the **object type** is `Dog` (what exists at runtime).

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python looks up every attribute at runtime (duck typing). Java's compiler refuses `a.fetch()` when `Animal` has no `fetch()`, even if the object really is a Dog.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: The compiler only knows that `x` is an Animal, and Animal has no `fetch()`. The object being a Dog doesn't matter at compile time. `((Dog) x).fetch()` would compile.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `a.x` reads the field by reference type A: 1. `a.getX()` is an overridden method, so B's runs and returns B's field: 2. `b.x` uses reference type B: 2. Same object, different field depending on the variable.

items: **Upcast** (subtype → supertype) is implicit and always safe: `Animal a = dog;`
**Downcast** (supertype → subtype) needs an explicit cast: `Dog d = (Dog) a;`
A downcast is checked at runtime. If the object isn't really that type: `ClassCastException`.
A cast never changes the object. It only changes how the compiler lets you use the reference.

blocks.caption: Compiles, but line 3 throws ClassCastException.

blocks.title: Impossible casts don't compile
blocks.text: Between two **classes**, the compiler rejects a cast that could never succeed: `(String) new Dog()` fails, because no object is both. Casting a non-final class to an **interface** compiles, since some subclass might implement it. A `final` class can only be cast to interfaces it implements.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
steps.explanation: The cast compiles: an Animal might be a Dog. At runtime the object is a Cat, so the JVM throws ClassCastException on line 7 and "done" is never printed.

steps.prompt: Given these types, which two statements compile? (They may still fail at runtime.) Choose two.
steps.explanation: A downcast from Animal to Dog compiles (and throws ClassCastException at runtime here). Dog is not final, so a subclass of Dog could implement Pet: the cast compiles. Rock is final and doesn't implement Pet, so that cast is impossible. Unrelated classes (Rock/Dog, String/Animal, Dog/String) can't be cast to each other.

blocks.text: Overriding is decided at runtime by the object. **Overloading** is decided at compile time by the declared types of the arguments.

blocks.code:
void feed(Animal a) { }  // chosen for
void feed(Dog d) { }     // declared types
Animal x = new Dog();
feed(x);   // feed(Animal)!

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Overload selection uses the compile-time type of the argument. `o` is declared Object, so `print(Object)` is chosen even though it holds a String. After the cast the argument type is String, so `print(String)` is chosen.

steps.prompt: A cast changes the type of the object on the heap.
steps.explanation: Objects never change type. A cast only changes the type of the **reference** the compiler sees, and a downcast adds a runtime check that may throw ClassCastException.

lessons.title: instanceof & pattern matching
lessons.summary: Type tests, binding variables and flow scoping.

blocks.text: `x instanceof T` is true when the object `x` refers to IS-A `T`. If `x` is `null`, the result is simply `false` (no exception).

blocks.caption: Prints true, false, false.

blocks.title: Impossible tests don't compile
blocks.text: If the compiler can prove the test can never be true, it's an error. `Integer n = 5; n instanceof String` fails: an Integer can never be a String. The same rule as casting.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
steps.explanation: `num instanceof Integer` is fine: a Number might be an Integer. But `n` is declared Integer, and Integer is a final class unrelated to String, so `n instanceof String` on line 5 can't compile.

blocks.text: If the test succeeds, the **binding variable** `s` is already cast to String and ready to use. No separate `(String) obj` cast.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: In Python you write `isinstance(obj, str)` and then use `obj` directly. Java's static typing needs a String-typed variable, and the pattern gives you one.

blocks.title: Generics in patterns
blocks.text: Type arguments are erased at runtime, so from an `Object` you can't test `instanceof List<String>`: that's a compile error. Use a wildcard, `List<?>`. A parameterized test is only allowed when the compiler can prove it safe, e.g. a `List<String>` tested against `ArrayList<String>`.
`s` is in scope only where the compiler knows the match **succeeded**.

items: `o instanceof String s && s.isEmpty()`: OK. The right side runs only if the match succeeded.
`o instanceof String s || s.isEmpty()`: compile error. The right side runs when the match **failed**.
`if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;` makes `s` usable **after** the if.
The binding name can't clash with an existing local variable.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: With `||`, the right side runs only when the left side is **false**, so `t` was never assigned. Line 2 is fine with `&&`. In lines 6–9, `u` is in scope in the `else` branch, where the match is known to have succeeded.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: `check(21)` matches Integer, so `i` is 21 and the result is "int 42". `"21"` is a String, so the negated test returns "no". `null instanceof Integer` is false (no NPE), so that's "no" too.

steps.prompt: Complete the pattern so the code prints 8.
steps.explanation: The syntax is `expr instanceof Type name`. The binding `n` can be used on the right of `&&` because that side only runs after a successful match. `isA` and `typeof` aren't Java.

steps.prompt: Given `Object o = "x";`, which two snippets compile? Choose two.
options: String s = "y"; if (o instanceof String s) { }
boolean b = o instanceof String s && s.isEmpty();
steps.explanation: The binding is usable inside the `if` that tested it and on the right of `&&`. With `||` or inside the negated branch the match failed, so `s` isn't in scope. A binding can't reuse the name of an existing local `s`. Integer can never be a String, so that test doesn't compile.

steps.prompt: `x instanceof Object` throws a NullPointerException when `x` is null.
steps.explanation: `instanceof` is null-safe: `null instanceof AnyType` is always `false`. That's why a pattern binding is never null.

blocks.text: A `sealed` class lists exactly which classes may extend it, using `permits`.

items: Every permitted subclass must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`.
`non-sealed` reopens the hierarchy: anyone may extend Poly.
Permitted subclasses must **directly** extend the sealed class.
They must be in the same package (or, with modules, the same named module).
`permits` may be left out when all subclasses are in the **same source file**.
A sealed class doesn't have to be abstract.

blocks.title: More sealed rules
blocks.text: A `sealed` class needs at least one permitted subclass: `sealed class Tool { }` with no subclasses in the file doesn't compile. `non-sealed` and `final` classes can't have a `permits` clause. You can't write `sealed` or `final` on an enum yourself (the compiler decides). Local and anonymous classes can never be permitted subtypes.

steps.prompt: Complete the hierarchy so that it compiles.
steps.explanation: `permits` requires a `sealed` type. Bike must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. Because Ebike (which has no modifier) extends it, only `non-sealed` works: `final` would block Ebike, and `sealed` would force Ebike itself to be final, sealed, or non-sealed. `abstract` alone doesn't satisfy the rule.

blocks.text: An ordinary class can be extended by anyone. A `final` class by no one. `sealed` sits in between: a **closed, known** set of subtypes.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python has no way to forbid subclassing at compile time. Java checks the whole sealed hierarchy when it compiles.

blocks.title: Missing modifier
blocks.text: A permitted subclass with **no** modifier (`class Pear extends Fruit`) does not compile. The compiler wants you to decide explicitly how the hierarchy continues.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Plum isn't listed in `permits`, so it can't extend Fruit, even though it's final. Nashi is fine: it extends Pear, which is `non-sealed`, so anyone may extend it.

items: Interfaces can be sealed. Permitted classes `implement` it; permitted interfaces `extend` it.
Records are implicitly `final`, so they satisfy the rule with no extra keyword.
Enums are implicitly final (or sealed), so they can implement a sealed interface too.
The payoff: the compiler knows **every** subtype, so a switch can be exhaustive without `default` (next lesson).

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Expect questions where one subclass forgets its modifier, or extends without being permitted. Check each class: is it permitted, and is it final / sealed / non-sealed?

steps.prompt: Which two statements about sealed types are true? Choose two.
options: Every permitted subclass must be final, sealed, or non-sealed.
A non-sealed subclass can be extended by classes that aren't listed anywhere.
A sealed class must be abstract.
A record can't implement a sealed interface.
The permits clause is required even when all subclasses are in the same file.
steps.explanation: Each permitted subclass picks one of the three modifiers (records and enums are final implicitly). `non-sealed` reopens that branch. A sealed class can be concrete, records commonly implement sealed interfaces, and `permits` can be inferred when everything is in one file.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: There is no `permits` clause, so the compiler infers the permitted subclasses from the same file: Dime and Nickel, both final. `c.cents()` dispatches to Dime (10), plus 5 from Nickel: the `+` adds two ints, giving 15.

steps.prompt: A record that implements a sealed interface must be explicitly marked `final`.
steps.explanation: Records are implicitly final, which already satisfies the sealed rule. Writing `final record` is allowed but redundant.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: Compilation fails because Pine is permitted but doesn't extend Tree.
Compilation fails because Tree must be abstract.
Compilation fails because Oak must be sealed.
steps.explanation: Every class in `permits` must actually extend the sealed class. Pine is final but doesn't extend Tree, so the permits clause is invalid. Oak is correct, and a sealed class may be concrete.

lessons.title: Pattern matching in switch
lessons.summary: Type patterns, guards, null, dominance, records.

items: Each `case` can test a type and bind a variable.
Cases are tried **top to bottom**.
A pattern switch must be **exhaustive**. On `Object` that means a `default` (or `case Object o`).

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python 3.10's `match` with `case int(i):` looks similar, but Java checks exhaustiveness and case order at **compile** time.

items: `when` adds a boolean guard to a pattern.
Without `case null`, a null selector throws `NullPointerException`, even when there's a `default`.
`case null, default ->` handles both in one label.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: 5 is an Integer but fails the guard `i > 9`, so the next case gives "s". 50 passes the guard: "B". "x" is a String: "S". 2.0 is a Double, matching only `default`: "?".

steps.prompt: What is the result?
steps.explanation: `default` does **not** match null. A switch on a null value throws NullPointerException unless it has a `case null` label.

blocks.text: A case is **dominated** when an earlier case already matches everything it could. That's a compile error, because the later case could never run.

items: Put more specific types first.
An unguarded `case String s` dominates a later `case String s when ...`.
A guarded case does **not** dominate a later unguarded case of the same type.
`default` goes after the pattern cases.

blocks.text: Java 21 also lets you mix **qualified enum constants** with type patterns when switching over a sealed interface (or `Object`). The constant must come **before** the type pattern that covers it.

blocks.title: Constant after the type
blocks.text: Swap the first two cases and it fails to compile: `case Light l` already matches every `Light`, so `case Light.RED` is dominated.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Every Long is a Number, so `case Number n` on line 6 already catches all Longs and `case Long l` can never run: it's dominated. Line 5 is fine because the guarded case on line 4 doesn't dominate it.

items: If the cases cover every permitted subtype, no `default` is needed.
Add a new permitted subtype later, and every such switch stops compiling until you handle it. That's a feature.
The same works for enums: covering every constant is exhaustive.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: Pet permits three types, but the switch only covers Dog and Cat. A pattern switch must be exhaustive, so without `case Bird b` or `default` it doesn't compile, even though `main` only passes a Dog.

items: A record pattern takes a record apart into its components, in declaration order.
Each component gets a type pattern: an explicit type or `var`.
Patterns nest: `Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point b)`.
The number of components must match the record exactly.
`null` never matches a record pattern.

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Java 21 has no unnamed pattern `_`. Every component needs a type (or `var`) and a name, even if unused.

blocks.title: Generic records infer their types
blocks.text: On a generic record you can leave the type arguments off the pattern. Against a `Pair<Integer, String>`, `Pair(var n, var s)` infers `Pair<Integer, String>`, so `n` is an `Integer` and `s` a `String`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: The Line is deconstructed into both Points and then into their coordinates: |4-1| + |6-2| = 3 + 4 = 7. A Point is not a Line, so `len(p)` falls to `default` and returns -1.

steps.prompt: Complete the switch so it prints `emptyhiother`.
steps.explanation: Guards use `when` (`&&` was only an old preview syntax). The two String cases don't cover a Box holding an Integer, so `default` is needed for exhaustiveness. `case null` would only handle a null Box, leaving the switch non-exhaustive.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about pattern-matching switch in Java 21 are true? Choose two.
options: Without `case null`, a null selector throws NullPointerException.
A switch over a sealed interface that covers all permitted subtypes needs no default.
Case order never matters because the compiler picks the most specific case.
`case Integer i && i > 0` is the syntax for a guard.
A record pattern can leave out components it doesn't need.
steps.explanation: Null needs an explicit `case null`. Sealed hierarchies make exhaustiveness checkable without `default`. Cases are tried in order (and out-of-order dominated cases don't compile). Guards use `when`, and a record pattern must list every component.

lessons.title: equals, hashCode & toString
lessons.summary: The Object contract and the equals overload trap.

steps.title: What every class inherits from Object

rows: an int derived from the object's identity

blocks.text: **equals contract**: reflexive (`a.equals(a)`), symmetric, transitive, consistent, and `a.equals(null)` is `false`.
**hashCode contract**: if `a.equals(b)`, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()`. The reverse isn't required: different objects may share a hash code.

blocks.title: Override both or neither
blocks.text: Override equals without hashCode, and two "equal" objects land in different HashSet buckets. Both get stored.

items: The parameter must be `Object`. The method must be `public`.
`instanceof` handles `null` for free: it returns false.
Records generate `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` from their components.

blocks.caption: Overloads equals. It does NOT override it.

blocks.text: The parameter type is `Point`, not `Object`, so this is a **new overload**. Collections like `List.contains` and `HashSet` call `equals(Object)`, which still compares identity. `@Override` would catch the mistake.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `a.equals(b)` with a Tag argument picks the overload `equals(Tag)`: true. With `o` declared Object, the compiler picks the inherited `equals(Object)`, which checks identity: false. `contains` also calls `equals(Object)`: false.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are required by the equals/hashCode contract? Choose two.
options: If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode().
If a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(), then a.equals(b) is true.
hashCode() returns a different value for every distinct object.
equals must take a parameter of the class's own type.
steps.explanation: Equal objects must have equal hash codes, and comparing with null gives false. Hash collisions between unequal objects are allowed. A parameter of the class's own type would overload, not override, equals.

steps.prompt: Adding `@Override` to `public boolean equals(Tag t)` causes a compile error.
steps.explanation: Object has no `equals(Tag)` method, so this method overrides nothing, and `@Override` makes that a compile error. That's exactly why you should always use it on equals.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Both Ids have hash code 1, so they land in the same bucket. HashSet then calls `equals`, which is still Object's identity check: they're different objects, so both are stored. Overriding hashCode alone is not enough.

steps.prompt: Complete a correct equals override.
steps.explanation: An override must take `Object`; `Money` would be an overload and `@Override` would reject it. The pattern `o instanceof Money m` checks the type, handles null, and gives a typed variable.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `toString()` is an overridden instance method, so the Cat version runs even through an Object reference. String concatenation calls it, and so does `List.toString()` for each element, inside brackets.

lessons.title: Interfaces
lessons.summary: Abstract, default, static and private members; conflicts.

items: A class `implements` any number of interfaces. An interface `extends` any number of interfaces.
No constructors, no instance fields, can't be `final`.
`protected` members are not allowed in interfaces.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python has no interfaces; the closest are `ABC` and `typing.Protocol`. Java default methods resemble mixins, but come with strict conflict rules.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Interface methods are implicitly `public`. Implementing one with package access makes it less visible, which is an illegal override. Writing `public String greet` fixes it. Using `PREFIX` is fine: it's an inherited constant.

steps.prompt: Which two lines compile inside `interface Tool { }`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Fields are constants (`public static final`), so they need a value. Private methods with a body are allowed since Java 9. `protected` isn't allowed, `default` and `static` can't be combined, and `final` makes no sense for an interface method.

items: Inheriting two defaults with the same signature: the class **must** override, or it doesn't compile.
`X.super.m()` calls interface X's default. X must be a direct superinterface.
**Class wins**: a method inherited from a superclass beats any interface default.
**More specific wins**: if B extends A and both define the default, B's is used.

blocks.text: `X.super.m()` is also illegal when **another** direct superinterface already overrides X's `m()`. Here Loud overrides Greeter's `hi()`, so Bot can't skip past it:

blocks.title: Re-abstracting a default
blocks.text: A subinterface may redeclare an inherited default as abstract: `String hi();`. Implementers must then provide it, and it counts as an abstract method, so an interface that was functional may stop being one.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: X gets `hi()` from both A and B, but B extends A and overrides it, so B's default is more specific: no conflict. Y inherits `hi()` from its superclass Base and from B; the class always wins.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: CatDog inherits two unrelated defaults named `name()`. Java won't pick one, so CatDog must override `name()` (and may call `Cat.super.name()`). The error is on the class declaration, line 7.

steps.prompt: Complete the method so Duck uses Walker's default `move()`.
steps.explanation: `Walker.super.move()` calls the default from the direct superinterface Walker. `Walker.this` would mean an enclosing instance, which doesn't exist, and `Duck.super` refers to Duck's superclass (Object), which has no `move()`.

blocks.title: Different from classes
blocks.text: A static method of a **class** is inherited by subclasses (`Child.parentStatic()` works). A static method of an **interface** is not. Always call it through the interface name.

blocks.title: Static can't hide a default
blocks.text: An interface can't declare a `static` method with the same signature as a `default` (or abstract) method it inherits. That's a compile error, not hiding.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: The default `tag()` is inherited, so line 7 is fine. The static `id()` is **not** inherited by Impl, so the unqualified call on line 9 fails. It must be `Util.id()`, as on line 8.

steps.prompt: A field declared in an interface can be reassigned by an implementing class.
steps.explanation: Interface fields are implicitly `public static final`: constants. Assigning to one anywhere is a compile error.

blocks.text: A **functional interface** has exactly one abstract method (SAM: single abstract method). A lambda can only be assigned to a functional interface type.

items: `default`, `static` and `private` methods don't count.
Abstract methods matching a public `Object` method (`equals(Object)`, `hashCode()`, `toString()`) don't count.
Inherited abstract methods **do** count.
`@FunctionalInterface` is optional. It makes the compiler enforce the rule.

steps.prompt: Which two interfaces are functional interfaces? Choose two.
options: interface A { void run(); default void x() { } }
interface C { void a(); void b(); }
interface D { String toString(); int size(); }
steps.explanation: A has one abstract method; the default doesn't count. D's `toString()` matches Object's public method, so only `size()` counts. B has none, C has two, and E's only method is an Object method, so it has zero abstract methods that count.

steps.prompt: Tap the line where javac reports the error.
steps.explanation: Pair has two abstract methods, so it's not a functional interface, and the `@FunctionalInterface` annotation on line 5 is rejected. Without the annotation, Pair would compile as a normal interface.

blocks.text: Common built-ins in `java.util.function`: `Supplier<T>` (`get`), `Consumer<T>` (`accept`), `Function<T,R>` (`apply`), `Predicate<T>` (`test`). Unit 7 covers them in depth.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Like `lambda x: x * 2`, but you can't call a Java lambda directly as `f(3)`. You call the interface's method: `f.apply(3)`.
A lambda implements only the **abstract** method. Default methods of the interface stay available on the lambda object and can call that abstract method.

blocks.title: Lambdas need a target type
blocks.text: `var f = x -> x * 2;` does not compile: a lambda has no type of its own. It needs a functional interface on the left, or a method parameter of that type.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `twice` applies `op` twice: `op(op(a, b), b)`. For add: (2+3)+3 = 8. For mul: (2*3)*3 = 18. The default method calls whichever lambda implements `op`.

steps.prompt: Complete the code so it prints `true`.
steps.explanation: Java lambdas use `->` (`=>` is JavaScript/C#, `:` is Python). A Predicate's abstract method is `test`; `apply` belongs to Function and `accept` to Consumer.

steps.prompt: Which lambda compiles as a `BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer>`?
steps.explanation: Two parameters need parentheses. You can't type only some parameters. A block body needs `return a + b;` with a semicolon. Only the first form is valid.

steps.prompt: An interface with one abstract method and three default methods is a functional interface.
steps.explanation: Only abstract methods count toward the single-abstract-method rule. Default, static and private methods are free.

lessons.title: Enums
lessons.summary: values, valueOf, ordinal, constructors, bodies, switch.

blocks.caption: Prints MEDIUM 1, LARGE, 3.

items: `values()` returns all constants in declaration order.
`valueOf("X")` is exact and case-sensitive. Unknown name: `IllegalArgumentException`.
`ordinal()` is the 0-based position. `name()` and `toString()` give the constant's name.
Each constant is a single object, so compare with `==`.
Enums can't extend a class (they already extend `java.lang.Enum`) but can implement interfaces. `new Size()` is illegal.

blocks.title: Python vs Java
blocks.text: Python's `Enum` members have `.name` and `.value`, and `Color["red"]` raises KeyError. Java has `name()` and `ordinal()`, and `valueOf` throws IllegalArgumentException.
Every enum implicitly implements `Comparable`. `compareTo` is `final` and compares by **ordinal**; OpenJDK returns the ordinal difference.

blocks.title: Same enum type only
blocks.text: `compareTo` takes the same enum type, so comparing a `Level` with a constant of another enum doesn't compile.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `values()` returns the constants in declaration order. `ordinal()` starts at 0. `int + String` is string concatenation, so each iteration prints the number followed by the name.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
steps.explanation: `valueOf` matches the constant name exactly, including case. There is no constant `red`, so it throws IllegalArgumentException. It never returns null.

items: Constants come first. A `;` ends the list when other members follow.
Enum constructors are implicitly `private`. Writing `public` or `protected` is a compile error.
Each constant's constructor runs exactly once, when the enum class is first used: all constants are created together.

steps.prompt: Tap the line that does not compile.
steps.explanation: Enum constructors can't be `public` or `protected`; they are always private (you never call them with `new`). Removing `public` makes the code compile.

steps.prompt: Complete the enum.
steps.explanation: A semicolon must end the constant list before fields or methods. The constructor is named after the enum and takes no `public` (illegal for enums). `void Level` would declare a method, leaving no constructor that accepts an int.

items: A constant can have its own body `{ ... }` that overrides methods.
If the enum declares an `abstract` method, **every** constant must implement it.
Otherwise constants override a normal method only when they want to.

blocks.text: A constant with a body is really an instance of an **anonymous subclass** of the enum. So its `getClass()` is not the enum class, but `getDeclaringClass()` is.

blocks.title: private isn't inherited
blocks.text: The body is a subclass, so `private` members of the enum aren't inherited there. Calling a private enum method from a constant body doesn't compile.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: RED and YELLOW have bodies that override `next()`. GREEN has no body, so it uses the enum's own `next()`, returning "WAIT". `values()` iterates in declaration order.

items: Case labels normally use the bare constant name: `case S`, not `case Size.S`.
A switch **expression** that covers every constant is exhaustive. Missing one without `default`: compile error.
An old-style switch **statement** on an enum doesn't have to cover every constant.
`EnumMap<Size, Integer>` is a fast Map keyed by an enum. It iterates in **ordinal order**, not insertion order.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about enums are true? Choose two.
options: An enum constructor can't be declared public.
Enum constants can be safely compared with ==.
An enum can extend another class.
`valueOf` returns null for an unknown name.
steps.explanation: Enum constructors are always private, and each constant is a singleton, so `==` is correct. Enums implicitly extend `java.lang.Enum`, so they can't extend anything else. `valueOf` throws IllegalArgumentException, and ordinals start at 0.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: EnumMap keeps its keys in the enum's **declaration** (ordinal) order: L, S, M. The order of `put` calls and the alphabet don't matter.

lessons.title: Nested classes
lessons.summary: Static nested, inner, local and anonymous classes.

rows: a class inside a method body

blocks.text: Nested classes can access the outer class's **private** members, and the outer class can access theirs.

items: A static nested class is like a top-level class that lives inside another. It can't use the outer **instance** fields directly.
Every inner object belongs to an outer object. Create it with `outer.new Inner()`, or just `new Inner()` inside an instance method of Outer.
Inside Inner, `Outer.this.x` reaches the outer object's field when a name is shadowed.
Since Java 16, inner classes may also declare static members.

steps.prompt: Create one Inner and one Nested object.
steps.explanation: An inner object needs an outer instance, so the syntax is `out.new Inner()`. A static nested class needs no outer object: `new Outer.Nested()`.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Plain `x` is the closest declaration: the parameter (3). `this.x` is the Inner object's field (2). `Outer.this.x` is the field of the enclosing Outer object (1).

steps.prompt: What is the result?
steps.explanation: `main` is static, so there is no Shop object. A static nested class (Receipt) needs no outer instance, so line 5 is fine. An inner class (Item) does, so `new Item()` on line 6 fails. `new Shop().new Item()` would work.

items: Local and anonymous classes (and lambdas) may use a local variable only if it is **final or effectively final**: never reassigned.
An anonymous class extends one class **or** implements one interface. It has no name and can't declare a constructor.
Local classes take no access modifier: `public class` inside a method fails.

blocks.title: Where the error appears
blocks.text: If a captured variable is changed later, javac reports the error at the line that **uses** it inside the class or lambda, not at the line that changes it.

steps.prompt: This code does not compile. Tap the line javac reports the error on.
steps.explanation: `count++` on line 9 means `count` is not effectively final. The rule is checked where the variable is captured, so javac reports "local variables referenced from an inner class must be final or effectively final" on line 6.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: The anonymous class extends the abstract Greeter and implements `greet()`. It captures `w`, which is effectively final. `twice()` calls `greet()` twice.

steps.prompt: Which two statements are true? Choose two.
options: Creating an inner class object requires an instance of the outer class.
An anonymous class can implement an interface.
A static nested class can directly read the outer class's instance fields.
An anonymous class can declare a constructor.
A local class can reassign a local variable it captured.
steps.explanation: Inner objects always belong to an outer object, and anonymous classes commonly implement an interface (or extend a class). Static nested classes have no outer instance. Anonymous classes have no name, so no constructor. Captured locals must be effectively final.

lessons.summary: 12 exam-style questions on inheritance, patterns, interfaces, enums.

blocks.text: Twelve exam-style questions covering the whole unit: constructor chaining, overriding, casting, patterns, sealed types, interfaces, enums and nested classes.

blocks.title: Exam technique
blocks.text: For every "What is the result?" question, check compilation first: access, modifiers, dominance, exhaustiveness, effectively final. Only then trace the output.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: `new B()` runs A's constructor first, which calls `print()`. That's overridden, so B's version runs, but B's field initializer `x = 5` hasn't run yet: it prints 0. Then the explicit `print()` call prints 5.

steps.prompt: Given `class P { void run() throws IOException { } }`, which two methods compile in `class C extends P`? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Wider access is fine, and an override may throw fewer or narrower checked exceptions. `Exception` is broader than `IOException`, `private` is weaker than package access, and changing the return type from `void` to `int` is incompatible.

steps.explanation: Sq(3) deconstructs to s = 3: 9. Rect(2, 2) matches the guarded case first because w == h: -1. Rect(2, 3) fails the guard and falls to the unguarded Rect case: 6. Both permitted types are covered, so no default is needed.

options: An exception is thrown at runtime
steps.explanation: A static method can't be overridden by an instance method (or the other way round). Declaring an instance `go()` in C with the same signature as P's static `go()` is a compile error on line 5.

steps.explanation: 3 is an Integer: +3. "four" is a String: +4. 5L is a Long, so the negated test is false and the `else` branch runs with `l` in scope: +5. null matches nothing, so `!(null instanceof Long l)` is true: +100. Total 112.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: The enum is initialized on first use, after "start" is printed. At that moment **all** constants are constructed in declaration order, so both GOLD and SILVER print, even though only SILVER is used. SILVER's ordinal is 1.

steps.prompt: Which two statements about interfaces are true? Choose two.
options: A static interface method is not inherited by implementing classes.
An interface field is implicitly public, static and final.
An interface can declare a protected abstract method.
A class inheriting two conflicting default methods compiles as long as it never calls them.
An interface can declare a constructor.
steps.explanation: Static interface methods must be called through the interface name, and interface fields are constants. `protected` isn't allowed in interfaces. A default-method conflict must be resolved by overriding, whether or not it's called. Interfaces have no constructors.

steps.prompt: What is the result?
steps.explanation: All casts compile: Apple and Pear are both Fruits, and Object can be cast to anything. `(Apple) o` succeeds at runtime because the object is an Apple. `(Pear) f` fails at runtime: the object is an Apple, not a Pear.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Each Step belongs to the Counter that created it. s1 and s2 both belong to `c`, so `c.n` becomes 2 + 2 = 4. The third Step belongs to `d`, so `d.n` is 2. Inner classes may access the private field `n`.

steps.prompt: What is the result of compiling and calling `f("")`?
steps.explanation: The unguarded `case String s` matches every String, so the guarded `case String s when ...` after it could never run. It is dominated, which is a compile error. Swapping the two cases fixes it.

steps.prompt: What is the output?
steps.explanation: Records generate equals and hashCode from their components, so the two `P(1)` objects are equal and the set keeps one. Q inherits identity-based equals, so both Q objects are stored. 1 + 2 = 3 elements.

steps.prompt: Given `sealed class Vehicle permits Car, Truck { }`, which two declarations compile (in the same file)? Choose two.
steps.explanation: Permitted subclasses must be final, sealed, or non-sealed. A plain or merely abstract Truck has none of these. Bus is not in the permits list, so it can't extend Vehicle at all.
